title: Rust Async, Demystified
summary: A dense field guide to Rust's async model: why futures do nothing until polled, what an await point really is, how runtimes and executors drive work, why Send bounds bite you, and what happens when you block inside async.

chapters.title: Lazy Futures: Nothing Runs Until Polled
points: `async fn` returns an anonymous type implementing `Future`; calling it runs zero user code
A future is a value, not a task — building one allocates state, performs no work
`let f = fetch(); // nothing happened yet` — work starts only at `f.await` or `spawn(f)`
Contrast: JS `Promise` is eager and hot; a constructed Promise is already executing
Contrast: Go goroutines start on `go f()`; Rust needs an explicit executor to poll
Unused-future footgun: `#[must_use]` warning `unused implementer of Future that must be used`
Dropping a future before completion silently cancels it — no code after the last poll runs
`Future` trait core: `fn poll(self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<Self::Output>`
`Poll::Pending` = not done, will wake later; `Poll::Ready(T)` = value produced
Laziness enables zero-cost composition: `timeout(select(a, b))` builds one state machine, no per-combinator allocation
Async blocks: `async { .. }` is also lazy; `async move { .. }` takes ownership of captures
Gotcha: side effects you expect at call time (logging, sending a request) are deferred to the first poll
Rule of thumb: a future is a recipe; the runtime is the cook

chapters.title: The State Machine Under async fn
points: The compiler desugars each `async fn` into an enum state machine, one variant per await point
Variants store the locals that live across an await; locals that don't are ordinary stack slots
Each `poll` call resumes at the last await point and runs forward until the next `Pending`
Futures are self-referential (a local borrowed across an await points into the same struct)
`Pin<&mut T>` exists to promise the future won't move after first poll, so those pointers stay valid
`Unpin` = safe to move anyway; most hand-written futures are `Unpin`, compiler-generated ones are not
`Box::pin(fut)` pins to the heap; `tokio::pin!(fut)` / `std::pin::pin!(fut)` pins on the stack
Future size = the max of all live-across-await state, not the sum; big futures cause stack blowups
Fix for a huge future: `Box::pin` it, or shrink locals held across awaits
Recursion needs indirection: `async fn` calling itself requires `Box::pin` or the `async_recursion` crate
Code example — desugared shape: `enum Fetch { Start, AwaitingBody { resp: Response }, Done }`
`.await` is not a syscall or thread yield — it is a `return Poll::Pending` from the state machine
No allocation per await: whole chain compiles into one flat struct (a key Rust-vs-GC-language win)

chapters.title: Await Points: Where Control Actually Yields
points: An await point is the only place an async fn can suspend — between them, execution is uninterrupted
`.await` on a ready future returns immediately; no yield, no scheduling
Cooperative scheduling: the runtime cannot preempt you; you must reach an await to give up the core
Cancellation happens only at await points — a dropped future stops between two awaits, never mid-statement
Cancel safety: `select!` may drop the losing branch; a partially-read buffer can be lost
Cancel-safe vs not: `AsyncReadExt::read` is cancel-safe, `read_exact` is not (may lose bytes)
Yield manually inside a long CPU loop: `tokio::task::yield_now().await`
Locks held across an await must be async locks — `std::sync::MutexGuard` is not `Send` and blocks peers
`tokio::sync::Mutex` is for guards held across awaits; prefer `std::sync::Mutex` for short non-await critical sections
Await points define the task's resume boundaries, so all state you need after must live in the future
Example gotcha: `for x in list { db.write(x).await; }` — cancellation can leave a partial write set
Await-in-loop is sequential; use `join_all` / `FuturesUnordered` for concurrency
`.await` in a non-async fn is a compile error: `await is only allowed inside async functions and blocks`

chapters.title: Wakers: How a Pending Future Gets Polled Again
points: `Context` carries one thing that matters: the `Waker`
Contract: return `Pending` ONLY after arranging for `waker.wake()` to be called later
A future that returns `Pending` without registering a waker hangs forever — the classic lost-wakeup bug
`waker.wake()` puts the task back on the executor's ready queue; it does not run it inline
`wake_by_ref()` avoids consuming the waker when you'll wake the same task repeatedly
Spurious wakeups are legal — poll must be idempotent and re-check its condition
Store the newest waker each poll: the task may have moved threads and the old waker is stale
Leaf futures (timers, sockets) hold the wakers; combinators just forward the `Context` down
Reactor role: epoll/kqueue/IOCP readiness event fires, reactor looks up the token, calls `wake()`
Manual future example — poll a flag, else `cx.waker().wake_by_ref(); Poll::Pending` (a busy-spin, deliberately)
`std::task::Waker` is a vtable-based type-erased handle: `RawWaker` + `RawWakerVTable`
`futures::task::AtomicWaker` for the common single-consumer register-and-wake pattern
Mental model: `Pending` is a promise to knock on the door later

chapters.title: Runtimes: Executor + Reactor
points: Rust ships the `Future` trait in std but NO runtime — you pick one
Executor: owns the ready queue, calls `poll` on tasks. Reactor: owns the OS event source, wakes tasks
Tokio = most common; multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler + `mio`-based reactor
async-std = std-shaped API; smol/`async-executor` = small and composable; embassy = embedded, no_std
`#[tokio::main]` desugars to `Runtime::new().block_on(async { .. })`
`block_on` drives one future to completion on the current thread; the bridge from sync to async
`tokio::spawn` hands a future to the executor, returns a `JoinHandle<T>` you can await or abort
Spawned tasks run even if you drop the handle; dropping a `JoinHandle` detaches, it does not cancel
Task ≈ green thread, but sized to the state machine (bytes), not a 8 MB stack — millions are feasible
Current-thread flavor: `Builder::new_current_thread()` — no `Send` bound needed via `spawn_local`
Work stealing: idle worker threads pull tasks from busy workers' queues to balance load
Runtime interop hazard: a Tokio timer/socket used under another runtime panics — `there is no reactor running`
Nesting `block_on` inside async panics: `Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime`
One runtime per process is the norm; passing a `Handle` beats creating a second

chapters.title: Concurrency Primitives: join, select, streams
points: Concurrency ≠ parallelism: `join!` interleaves on one task; `spawn` can use many cores
`tokio::join!(a, b)` polls both to completion in the current task, returns a tuple
`try_join!` short-circuits on the first `Err`
`tokio::select!` races branches, returns the first ready, DROPS the rest — read the cancel-safety table
`select!` in a loop needs `&mut fut` or a pinned future, or you restart the branch each iteration
`FuturesUnordered` / `futures::stream::iter(..).buffer_unordered(n)` bounds in-flight concurrency
`join_all(v)` runs N futures in one task — fine for I/O, useless for CPU parallelism
Fan-out with parallelism: `spawn` each, then await the `JoinHandle`s
`Stream` = async `Iterator`; `poll_next` yields `Poll<Option<T>>`; consume with `while let Some(x) = s.next().await`
Channels: `mpsc` (bounded backpressure), `oneshot` (single reply), `broadcast` (fan-out), `watch` (latest value)
Backpressure comes free from a bounded `mpsc` — `send().await` suspends when the queue is full
`CancellationToken` + `select!` is the idiomatic graceful-shutdown pair
Timeouts: `tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(5), fut).await` returns `Err(Elapsed)`

chapters.title: Send, Sync, and 'static: Why the Compiler Yells
points: `tokio::spawn` requires `F: Future + Send + 'static` and `F::Output: Send`
A future is `Send` iff every value held ACROSS an await point is `Send`
Classic error: `future cannot be sent between threads safely ... held across an await point`
`Rc<T>` / `RefCell<T>` across an await kills `Send`; use `Arc<T>` / `tokio::sync::Mutex`
`std::sync::MutexGuard` is `!Send` — scope it in a block that ends before the await, or use an async mutex
Fix pattern: `let v = { let g = m.lock().unwrap(); g.clone() }; use(v).await;`
`'static` doesn't mean 'lives forever' — it means 'borrows nothing from the caller'
Fix for `'static`: clone the data or move an `Arc` into the async block
Non-`Send` work belongs on `spawn_local` inside a `LocalSet`, or on a dedicated current-thread runtime
Auto traits leak through async fn: you cannot write `impl Future + Send` on a trait method's return without help
`async fn` in traits (stable since 1.75) returns an anonymous type with no `Send` bound; use `trait_variant` or `#[async_trait]` to get one
`#[async_trait]` boxes the future — one heap allocation and dynamic dispatch per call
Debug trick: assert it early with `fn assert_send<T: Send>(_: T) {}` on the future

chapters.title: Blocking Inside Async: The Cardinal Sin
points: A blocked poll occupies its worker thread — no other task on that thread can run
Tokio's multi-thread runtime defaults to one worker per core; N blocking calls stall N cores
Symptoms: latency spikes, timers firing late, heartbeats missed, throughput cliff under load
Offenders: `std::thread::sleep`, `std::fs`, `reqwest::blocking`, synchronous DB drivers, `Mutex` contention
Also blocking: heavy CPU work — parsing a 200 MB JSON, hashing a password, image resize
`tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| ..)` moves it to a separate blocking pool (default cap 512 threads)
`rayon` for data-parallel CPU work; bridge back with a `oneshot` channel
`block_in_place` converts the current worker thread (multi-thread runtime only) — a blunt escape hatch
Never `Handle::block_on` inside an async fn: panics, or deadlocks if the runtime is single-threaded
Detection: `tokio-console`, or the unstable runtime metrics / `--cfg tokio_unstable` task poll-time histogram
Rule of thumb: any poll taking >10–100 µs should be broken up or moved off the runtime
Async file I/O is a lie on Linux — `tokio::fs` is `spawn_blocking` under the hood
Password hashing example: `argon2` at ~100 ms per call will destroy a 4-core runtime at 40 requests/s

chapters.title: Costs, Trade-offs, and When Not To Use Async
points: Async wins on I/O-bound, high-concurrency workloads: 10k+ sockets, proxies, chat, scrapers
Threads win on CPU-bound work, low connection counts, and simple blocking scripts
Memory: OS thread ≈ 8 MB virtual stack reserve; async task = size of its state machine, often <1 KB
Context switch: thread switch ≈ 1–5 µs through the kernel; task switch ≈ tens of ns, a function return
Latency cost: an await adds a poll and a possible queue hop; a hot path with no I/O is faster sync
Compile-time cost: deep future nesting produces large monomorphized types and slow builds
Debuggability cost: stack traces show executor frames, not your logical call chain
'Function coloring': async infects callers; a sync trait cannot call async code without `block_on`
Ecosystem split: a crate must pick tokio vs smol vs async-std traits (`AsyncRead` differs between futures-rs and tokio)
`async` in libraries: stay runtime-agnostic where possible, or feature-gate the runtime
Don't go async for a CLI that makes 3 HTTP calls — `ureq` and threads are simpler and faster to write
Comparison row: throughput ↑, tail latency ↑ if you block, complexity ↑↑, memory ↓↓

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and the Full Picture
points: Forgetting `.await` — the future is built and dropped; nothing happens, only a `must_use` warning
Awaiting inside a loop when you meant concurrency — N sequential round-trips instead of one wave
Holding a `std::sync` lock across an await — `!Send` error, or a stalled worker
Blocking on the runtime thread — the #1 production incident cause in async Rust
Unbounded `mpsc` or unbounded `spawn` — no backpressure, memory grows until OOM
Ignoring `select!` cancel safety — silently dropped reads and partial writes
Spawning without ever awaiting the `JoinHandle` — panics inside the task are swallowed
Assuming `spawn` runs immediately — it queues; the task may not start before you await something else
Detached tasks outliving shutdown — use a `TaskTracker` / `JoinSet` and await them on exit
Nesting runtimes or mixing runtime types — the `no reactor running` panic
Async-in-trait without a `Send` bound, then failing to `spawn` the resulting future
Checklist to internalize: lazy until polled · await = suspend point · waker = the callback · runtime = executor + reactor · `Send` = safe across await · never block the poll
Debug toolkit: `tokio-console` for task state, `RUST_BACKTRACE` plus `#[track_caller]`, `tracing` spans that survive awaits
